*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Solomon son of David strengthened himself over his kingdom.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause (note the vav [ו] + subject pattern) probably has a causal nuance here.

*Translator's note:* Or “high place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the tent of meeting of God.”

*Study note:* The tabernacle was located in Gibeon; see 1 Chr 21:29.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your word.”

*Translator's note:* Or “be firm, established.”

*Translator's note:* The cohortative with prefixed vav (ו) following the imperative here indicates purpose/result.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so I may go out before this nation and come in.” The expression “go out…and come in” here means “to lead” (see *HALOT* 425 s.v. יצא qal.4).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who is able?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “no one.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to judge.”

*Translator's note:* The words “as plentiful” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he made.”

*Study note:* The foothills (שְׁפֵלָה, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

*Study note:* Because *Que* is also mentioned, some prefer to see v. 16-17 as a reference to Mutsur. Que and Mutsur were located in Cilicia or Cappadocia (in modern southern Turkey). See *HALOT* 625 s.v. מִצְרַיִם.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they brought up and brought out from Egypt a chariot for 600 silver (pieces), and a horse for 150, and in the same way to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram by their hand they brought out.”

*Study note:* Beginning with 2:1, the verse numbers through 2:18 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (*BHS*), with 2:1 ET = 1:18 HT, 2:2 ET = 2:1 HT, 2:3 ET = 2:2 HT, etc., through 2:18 ET = 2:17 HT. Beginning with 3:1 the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Huram.” Some medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate spell the name “Hiram,” agreeing with 1 Chr 14:1. “Huram” is a variant spelling referring to the same individual.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cedars.” The word “logs” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who retains strength to build for him a house, for the heavens and the heavens of heavens do not contain him? And who am I that I should build for him a house, except to sacrifice before him?”

*Translator's note:* This is probably a variant name for almug trees; see 9:10-11 and the parallel passage in {{1 Kings 10:11|1 Kgs 10:11-12}}; cf. NLT. One or the other probably arose through metathesis of letters.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “know.”

*Study note:* As a unit of dry measure a *cor* was roughly equivalent to six bushels (about 220 liters).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “20,000 baths” (also a second time later in this verse). A bath was a liquid measure roughly equivalent to six gallons (about 22 liters), so this was a quantity of about 120,000 gallons (440,000 liters).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Huram” (also in v. 12). Some medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate spell the name “Hiram,” agreeing with 1 Chr 14:1. “Huram” is a variant spelling referring to the same individual.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who has given to King David a wise son knowing discernment and insight, who will build a house for the Lord and house for his kingship.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Solomon counted.”

*Study note:* The term גֵּר (ger) refers to a foreign resident, but with different social implications in different settings. In Mosaic Law the resident foreigner was essentially a naturalized citizen and convert to worshiping the God of Israel (see {{Exodus 12:19|Exod 12:19}}, {{Exodus 12:48|48}}; {{Deuteronomy 29:10|Deut 29:10-13}}).

*Translator's note:* In {{2 Samuel 24:16|2 Sam 24:16}} this individual is called אֲרַוְנָא (ʾaravna; traditionally “Araunah”). The form of the name found here also occurs in 1 Chr 21:15; 18-28.
*Study note:* This would be April-May, 966 b.c. by modern reckoning.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and these are the founding of Solomon to build the house of God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the length [in] cubits by the former measure was 60 cubits, and a width of 20 cubits.” Assuming a length of 18 inches (45 cm) for the standard cubit, the length of the foundation would be 90 feet (27 m) and its width 30 feet (9 m).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and the porch which was in front of the length corresponding to the width of the house, 20 cubits.” The phrase הֵיכַל הַבַּיִת (hekhal habbayit, “the main hall of the temple,” which appears in the parallel account in {{1 Kings 6:3|1 Kgs 6:3}}) has been accidentally omitted by homoioarcton after עַל־פְּנֵי (’al pene, “in front of”). Note that the following form, הָאֹרֶךְ (haʿorekh, “the length”), also begins with the Hebrew letter he (ה). A scribe’s eye probably jumped from the initial *he* on הֵיכַל to the initial he on הָאֹרֶךְ, leaving out the intervening letters in the process.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has “one hundred and 20 cubits,” i.e., (assuming a cubit of 18 inches) 180 feet (54 m). An ancient Greek witness and the Syriac version read “20 cubits,” i.e., 30 feet (9 m). It is likely that מֵאָה (meʾah, “a hundred”) should be emended to אַמּוֹת (ʾammot, “cubits”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “covered.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the large house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wood of evergreens.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he put up on it palm trees and chains.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he plated the house [with] precious stone for beauty, and the gold was the gold of Parvaim.”

*Study note:* The location of *Parvaim*, the source of the gold for Solomon’s temple, is uncertain. Some have identified it with modern Farwa in Yemen; others relate it to the Sanskrit parvam and understand it to be a general term for the regions east of Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the house of the holy place of holy places.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “20 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), this would give a length of 30 feet (9 m).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “20 cubits.” Some suggest adding, “and its height 20 cubits” (see {{1 Kings 6:20|1 Kgs 6:20}}). The phrase could have been omitted by homoioteleuton.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word כִּכַּר (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the gold plating was 40,380 lbs. (18,360 kg).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the wings of the cherubim, their length was 20 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the wingspan of the cherubim would have been 30 feet (9 m).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the wing of the one was 5 cubits from the touching of the wall of the house, and the other wing was 5 cubits from the touching of the wing of the other cherub.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), each wing would have been 7.5 feet (2.25 m) long.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the wing of the one (הָאֶחָד, haʾekhad, “the one”; this should probably be emended to הָאַחֵר, haʾakher, “the other”) cherub was 5 cubits, touching the wall of the house, and the other wing was 5 cubits, clinging to the wing of the other cherub.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the wings of these cherubim were spreading 20 cubits.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they were standing on their feet, with their faces to the house.” An alternative translation of the last clause would be, “with their faces to the main hall.”

*Study note:* The figure given here appears to refer to the combined length of both pillars (perhaps when laid end-to-end on the ground prior to being set up; cf. v. 17); the figure given for the height of the pillars in {{1 Kings 7:15|1 Kgs 7:15}}, {{2 Kings 25:17|2 Kgs 25:17}}, and Jer 52:21 is half this (i.e., 18 cubits).

*Text-critical note:* The Syriac reads “18 cubits” (27 feet). This apparently reflects an attempt at harmonization with {{1 Kings 7:15|1 Kgs 7:15}}, {{2 Kings 25:17|2 Kgs 25:17}}, and Jer 52:21.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he made before the house two pillars, 35 cubits [in] length, and the plated capital which was on its top [was] 5 cubits.” The significance of the measure “35 cubits” (52.5 feet or 15.75 m, assuming a cubit of 18 inches) for the “length” of the pillars is uncertain. According to {{1 Kings 7:15|1 Kgs 7:15}}, each pillar was 18 cubits (27 feet or 8.1 m) high. Perhaps the measurement given here was taken with the pillars lying end-to-end on the ground before they were set up.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text adds here, “in the inner sanctuary,” but the description at this point is of the pillars, not the inner sanctuary.

*Translator's note:* Or “one on the south and the other on the north.”

*Translator's note:* The name “Yakin” appears to be a verbal form and probably means, “he establishes.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the name “Boaz” is uncertain. For various proposals, see BDB 126-27 s.v. בֹּעַז. One attractive option is to revocalize the name as בְּעֹז (beʿoz, “in strength”) and to understand it as completing the verbal form on the first pillar. Taking the words together and reading from right to left, one can translate the sentence, “he establishes [it] in strength.”

In this case the temple is referred to as a “house” where the Lord himself can reside.
